IB RESOURCE SPOTLIGHT

12:25–12:30

Making the abstract explicit

The role of metacognition in teaching and learning

What is it?

A four-page IB research brief by Beach and colleagues (2021).

Where is it?

Public IB website → Research → Metacognition.

Open the research page ↗

Why might it help?

It explores how teachers make learning processes explicit through modelling, questions and reflection.

Open the research brief ↗

Start on page 2
“What role do teachers play?”

Page 3: classroom practice
Page 4: ownership and seeking help

IB-commissioned research, not assessment rules. Metacognition connects with thinking and self-management; it is not the whole self-management category.

Use the familiar what/where/why format. Show access and identify a short starting section. Do not lecture through all four pages or pre-select the strategy groups should use.

Source: Beach et al. (2021), research brief, pages 2–4. Page 4 explicitly includes help-seeking in learner ownership. The public landing page dates the research to 2021.

The source summary accessible from the toolbar is a short facilitator paraphrase, not an extract or a new IB requirement. The deck works offline; external sources need a connection.

PROFESSIONAL LEARNING

12:30–12:33

What do we mean by self-management?

Self-management is not just meeting deadlines, doing homework and studying.

WHAT WE OFTEN NOTICE

Meeting deadlines

Completing homework

Studying

Staying organised

WHAT STUDENTS ALSO NEED TO LEARN

Make decisions
Plan and prioritise

Choose strategies
Respond when stuck

Monitor progress
Reflect and adapt

Manage attention
Regulate emotions

Use feedback
Decide what to change

Seek help
Ask a focused question

Think of a recent moment when a student needed you to decide what to do next.

Classroom examples for today’s inquiry; several connect self-management with thinking skills. Sources are available below.

Anis confirmed that teacher and student input identified self-management and thinking as the two priorities. Focus on self-management today, while recognising overlap with thinking skills.

The right-hand examples are our classroom framing, not a verbatim IB classification. Avoid reducing self-management either to compliance or to metacognition alone. No need to explain the entire ATL framework.

Give only a brief invitation to recall an episode; the task includes a quiet minute for everyone to think. Continue to the support question rather than asking for a long plenary.

THE DISCUSSION

Continue to the group task by 12:33

Can there be too much help?

A QUESTION RAISED IN IB RESEARCH

A 2017 study reported that one school was reconsidering how much support it provided after an external reviewer questioned whether students had enough opportunity to think for themselves.

Barnett, Avila & Aklog (2017), p. 22 · paraphrase ↗

When might this support
be needed?

What is it helping the student access or learn?

When might it take over
a learner decision?

What will the student get to decide or practise?

What would you need to know before deciding?Prior teaching · subject knowledge · task demands · learner needs

One reported school discussion, not proof that less help is always better. Appropriate support and help-seeking remain important.

The school episode really appears on page 22 of Barnett, Avila and Aklog, March 2017. The on-screen wording is a paraphrase. This is not an official IB workshop scenario or a validated claim that reducing support improves learning.

Keep the question open. Avoid sorting teacher actions into good/bad in advance. Ask what was already taught, whether missing subject knowledge or inaccessible instructions are the actual obstacle, and which learner decision is being developed.

Do not imply that reminders, co-regulation, disability accommodations or accessible scaffolds should simply be removed. Fading support is conditional on the learner and the task; useful supports can continue. Fewer questions to the teacher is not the default success measure.

For assessed work, subject-specific guidance about feedback and authenticity still applies. A discussion of self-management does not authorise extra IA/EE assistance.

GROUP INQUIRY · CHART PAPER + MARKERS

12:33–12:47 · 14 minutes

How much support is appropriate?

Think individually for 1 minute. Then choose one scenario to explore as a group.

AThe weekly checklist

An IA student falls behind. The teacher gives a weekly checklist, Friday check-ins and reminders of the next task. The student meets the next two checkpoints.

BTwo possible directions

Ten minutes remain. A student is stuck on an extended response. After guiding questions, the teacher suggests two directions. The student chooses one and continues.

CThree feedback priorities

After students struggle to use feedback on a practice task, the teacher identifies three changes for each response. Students revise, and the work improves.

DThe shared timetable

A student misses CP project deadlines. Teacher and student build a timetable with twice-weekly check-ins. The student says these help and asks to continue them.

Fictional facilitator-created scenarios, not official IB cases. More than one response may be defensible.

Discuss

How might the support help? What might it limit?

What extra information could change your view? Consider what the student needs to learn.

Research

Use the IB brief (pp. 2–4) to challenge or develop one idea. You may consult another source.

Distinguish experience, source guidance and a proposal to test.

Write on your chart

Keep / change / gradually hand over — and why.

Teacher action → what students practise.
One sign of ownership.
One uncertainty to test.

Before you finish

Try 30–60 seconds of your teaching in one subject context.
Which decision would students practise making? Keep student examples anonymous.

Leave this complete task on screen

The four cases and all discuss/research/write/rehearse instructions are on this one page. A printable copy is available from the toolbar. Cases are fictional, facilitator-created prompts, not IB materials, and there is no answer key.

Suggested pacing within 14 minutes: 1 minute individual thought; 4 minutes choose/discuss one case; 3 minutes focused source consultation; 5 minutes develop and record one teaching response; 1 minute rehearse. These are facilitation cues, not a series of additional slides.

Research starting point: IB metacognition brief, pages 2–4. The toolbar’s source summary can support discussion if the connection fails. AI may be used to question or adapt an idea, not as an unchecked source or with identifiable student information.

Prompts while circulating

“What would change your mind?” “Which part needs teaching?” “Would this help a novice and an experienced learner in the same way?” “How would you know the plan or strategy belongs to the student?” “Could this be a subject-knowledge or access issue rather than self-management?”

In case A, distinguish planning scaffolds from doing assessed work. Case C concerns a practice task, so it is not a claim about permitted IA feedback. In case D, honour the student’s perspective; ongoing check-ins are not automatically inappropriate.

Do not force consensus. Ask groups to keep one disagreement or uncertainty visible. The output is one plausible approach to teaching a learner decision, not a comprehensive self-management framework.

First six minutes: move to relevant charts, read, discuss and leave a useful comment. There is no requirement to visit every chart and no vote for the most popular strategy.

At 12:53, ask everyone to return. Reserve the final two minutes for revision. When a group sees something differently, encourage it to explain what assumptions produce that judgement.

SYNTHESIS AND CLOSE

12:55–1:00

What would we take into the classroom?

01

When does support help students make decisions — and when might it make decisions for them?

02

What still needs to be tried or understood in real classrooms?

ONE MINUTE · PERSONAL NOTE

One possible next step

In a suitable lesson, I might try…

I would look for…

Or: I need to understand… before choosing an approach.

Today’s ideas will inform our ATL work and the future PDP.

Use about three minutes for a small number of contributions, one minute for the private note, and one minute to close. No round of formal presentations or collection of personal commitments.

Suggested close: “We are identifying approaches worth trying and questions worth investigating. Classroom experience will help us decide what deserves further development in our ATL work and, later, the PDP.”

After the meeting: photograph the revised charts without identifiable student details. Synthesize recurring situations, proposed teaching responses and uncertainties. Preserve disagreement. These are evidence of professional inquiry and proposed practice, not evidence that student self-management has improved.

A later relevant session can revisit ordinary classroom examples; no new date or compulsory implementation deadline is being created here.

Sources and scope

Sources and use

This is SISJ professional learning, informed by IB resources. The four discussion cases are fictional facilitator-created examples, not official IB workshop cases. They have no official IB answer key.

1. Metacognition research brief

Beach, P. T., Anderson, R. C., Jacovidis, J. N., and Chadwick, K. L. (2021). Making the abstract explicit: the role of metacognition in teaching and learning. IB-commissioned research. Read pp. 2–4.

Open the four-page brief · Publication page

Offline starting point — facilitator paraphrase

The brief links planning, monitoring and reflection. It describes teachers making thinking visible and helping learners use reflection to adjust their approach. It also recognises appropriate help-seeking as part of ownership.

Use this to question your proposed support, not as a formula for how much help every learner should receive.

2. Academic mindsets study

Barnett, E., Avila, O., and Aklog, F. (March 2017). An analysis of the development of positive academic mindsets in diverse IBO schools. NCREST, Teachers College, Columbia University. The school discussion used on slide 6 is on p. 22.

Open report at page 22

This is a reported school discussion; it does not establish that less support is always better.

3. IB approaches to teaching and learning overview

The public IB overview presents ATL as deliberate skills, strategies and attitudes, and teaching as inquiry-based, collaborative and differentiated. It is historical background, not current evaluation or assessment requirements.

Open the two-page overview

Assessment boundary: For IA or other assessed work, check the current subject-specific rules on permitted feedback and assistance. These scenarios do not replace those rules.

School information: The housekeeping dates and approved poster were supplied or approved by Anis. They are school guidance, not IB-wide deadlines or mandated MYP-to-DP equivalences.
